lesson.title: Back it up
lesson.subtitle: Lose a phone, not your work

video.title: Back it up
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds; narration in the lesson language, captions as separate files.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: Three copies, two kinds, one away

scenes.visual: School yard at break. Amina holds a dripping phone over a bucket of water. Thought bubbles: a photo album, a marks book, a contact list.
scenes.animation: Drips fall; bubbles pop one by one.
scenes.narration: My phone slipped into a bucket of water at break. Three years of class photos, my marks, every parent’s number. Is it all gone?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the cyber track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how to lose a phone, but not your work.

scenes.visual: Four small disasters: a phone left on a bus seat, a phone in water, a laptop with a dark screen beside an exam calendar, a folder wrapped in a padlock with a ransom note.
scenes.animation: Each disaster card flips in, 400 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Phones get lost, stolen and dropped in water. Laptops die, often the week before exams. And ransomware is malware that locks your files and asks for money to open them. A backup is a second copy, kept somewhere else, so one bad day doesn’t take everything.

scenes.visual: Clean card: the numbers 3, 2 and 1 stand up one after another; under them, three file copies, a phone and a cloud, and a house far from the school.
scenes.animation: Numbers bounce in as they are said.
scenes.narration: Professionals use the three-two-one rule. Three copies of what matters. On two different kinds of storage, like your phone and the cloud. And one copy away from school, so a fire or a flood can’t take them all.

scenes.visual: A teacher’s desk: a register, lesson plans, an exam paper, a class photo and a phone contact list slide into a cloud labelled “Every night”.
scenes.animation: Items slide into the cloud one by one; a moon appears.
scenes.narration: So what matters? Marks and registers. Lesson plans and exam papers. Class photos, and your contacts, with every parent’s number. Turn on your phone’s automatic backup, and your chat app’s backup, so it happens every night without you.

scenes.visual: Two columns. Left: a phone and a cloud linked by sync arrows; a file is crossed out on the phone, and the cross appears in the cloud too. Right: a USB drive on a shelf, its cable unplugged.
scenes.animation: The cross copies across the sync arrow; the USB cable swings free.
scenes.narration: Careful: syncing isn’t the same as a backup. If a file is deleted or locked on your phone, the synced copy can be deleted or locked too. Version history helps, because you can go back to yesterday’s copy. But one copy should always sit unplugged, on a USB drive or an external disk.

scenes.visual: Joseph in the school office beside a computer showing a padlock screen. Two USB drives on the desk: one plugged in, one in a drawer labelled “Friday”. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check. Ransomware locks the school office computer. There’s a USB drive still plugged in, and another that was unplugged after Friday’s backup. Which copy saves you?

scenes.visual: The “unplugged after Friday” card gets the check badge. The plugged-in drive turns grey with a padlock; files flow back from the Friday drive.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; files stream back.
scenes.narration: The one unplugged after Friday. Ransomware locks everything it can reach, so the plugged-in drive and the synced folder are locked too. Report it, don’t pay, and restore Friday’s copy onto a clean computer.

scenes.visual: A calendar with one day circled each term. A hand opens a file from a USB drive; a check mark appears.
scenes.animation: Calendar pages turn; the file opens; check pops.
scenes.narration: A backup you’ve never opened is only a hope. Once a term, open one file from your backup and check it’s all there. Then you know it works before the bad day comes.

scenes.visual: A file and its copy each get a fingerprint stamp. The stamps match. Then one letter in the copy changes, and its fingerprint changes completely.
scenes.animation: Fingerprint stamps press down; the changed stamp scrambles.
scenes.on_screen_text: How a computer checks a copy
scenes.narration: How does a computer know a copy is exact? It makes a fingerprint of each file, called a hash. Change one letter, and the fingerprint changes completely. You’ll make some yourself in the lab.

scenes.visual: Amina holds up her phone with a cloud icon beside it. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. I keep my marks on my phone, with a copy in the cloud. Do I meet the three-two-one rule?

scenes.visual: The “not yet” card gets the check badge; a USB drive joins the phone and the cloud. Four summary cards line up.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Not yet: that’s only two copies. Add a third, on a USB drive kept at home. Remember: three copies, two kinds of storage, one away from school, one unplugged, and a test restore every term.

scenes.visual: Joseph’s classroom. Groups draw a school, a home and a cloud on paper, with arrows between them; one group circles the home copy.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: tell the story of a lost phone. Groups draw where three copies of the class register could live, and circle the one that would survive a flood.

checkpoints.prompt: Ransomware locks the office computer. Which backup saves you?

options.text: The USB drive that was still plugged in
The USB drive unplugged after Friday’s backup
The folder that syncs with the computer

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: ransomware can’t reach a drive that isn’t connected. Restore Friday’s copy onto a clean computer.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: ransomware locks everything it can reach, including a plugged-in drive and a synced folder. The unplugged copy saves you.

checkpoints.prompt: Marks on the phone and a copy in the cloud. Does that meet the 3-2-1 rule?

options.text: No: add a third copy, unplugged and away from school

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: that’s two copies. A USB drive kept at home completes the rule.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the rule is three copies. Add a third, on a USB drive kept at home.
